title: Are you clinging to the TUI to feel like a developer?
content: Or, are you (really) still more productive in the TUI? Does curating the perfect set of shell programs in a multiplexer help you write better code? Ship stuff quicker?

comments.content:
Fwiw, wince the advent of coding agents being useful, I am even more in the TUI than before. Because the text is native.

But I have been enjoying the mobile apps - claude-code remote sessions are very nice when Claude ca show you designs before you approve and I am currently experimenting with herdr.

I wouldn't mind better conversation? I might want to try https://github.com/eliasstravik/herdr-call

But when agents unravel, I am opening my shell, in tmux or zellij, with my overconfigured zsh and atuin and I can still troubleshoot. There is no better escape hatch.

No. Once I found a web client that does what I want (paseo), I hard forked it and built out the features I want.

I touch vscode occasionally when I know explaining a simple thing to an LLM will take forever, but eventually hard fork will handle all the types of media I want to produce and it'll be the only one stop shop for development.
I don't think it's about feeling like a developer.

What is the alternative workflow? I didn't realise the terminal was already outdated. I assume some sort of orchestration layer is now the norm? I'd be interested to hear what developer are using for this.

I’m used to editing in nvim, even if it’s markdown for an agent. Or looking at agent code. I will on occasion run the agents code on my own in a CLI. Or make a small git commit.

Plus GUIs are distracting and not conducive to focus. They’re usually opinionated about one way of doing work. Sure if you do that work, it’s great. But the CLI is the most flexible / unopinionated.

By TUI do you just mean “the terminal”, or do you mean “a specific user interface built in the terminal, such as far or Claude code”?

If the former, that’s always been true and nothing has changed recently to challenge it. If the latter, I’m not.

>...help you write better code? Ship stuff quicker?

Nope, but it's comfier.

I know you didn't mention coding agents, but LLMs are so good at understanding T(ext)UIs. Sure you can just add screenshots in agent sessions, but it's way easier for the agent to run `herdr pane read` by itself.

"AI" just didn't click for me when ChatGPT first launched, and claude-desktop/cursor/codex/windsurf all were inconvenient and un-fun. It was only when I started piping tmux scrollback buffer into claude-code (and now Pi) that I started enjoying "coding" again.

Some terminal emulators are still simpler with less data in ram and therefore higher cpu cache residency.

Nice and fast like typing into 8-bit BASIC.

And today the CPU is fast , too.

80x25 doesn’t need too much of a GPU, which avoids long 300ms PCIe network operations.

Low latency is King.

EDIT: typo
The question is giving 1995, aka “The time has come to travel beyond Windows 3.1 and MS-DOS, into the world of Microsoft Windows 95” — Windows 95 promo text.
Am I allowed to enjoy my job, or is that not allowed anymore?

Exactly, it seems like nerds forgotten we live in a free country.

Use whatever that makes you productive.

If I have to work on a certain software for a long time, I prefer a GUI. If I am working on a small software that I wrote myself, I prefer a TUI because it is lighter and I am very familiar with how to use the software I wrote.

The thing is, that the shell can be quite fast. Not in terms of pure speed, but in terms of interaction. Yes GUI can expose a lot of actions, especially chainable ones like listing results and acting on one of the items. But if I know the exact thing I need, a shell script would be faster. The only thing faster is a set of keyboard shotcuts (think vim, magit, w3m,...).

When I'm working on a project for some time ($JOB), I usually end up writing little utilities and makefiles to speed up common tasks. Especially if they are some things I need to do on a regular basis. Sometimes it doesn't pay out in the end. But the whole flow is smoother and thus more delightful.

As far as TUI programs go, my interest is mostly in remote machine use and the ubiquity of shortcuts. Old GUI used to have a lot of shortcuts (Just checked and QT in KDE stil supports Alt based navigation (I forgot the exact name)), but now it's just icons and non visible keybindings. Also most TUI can easily shell out to other utilities making integration easy.

To recap: I code better when I have smoother workflow, which means easy access to the information I need now (next error from the last run, docs for the current function,...). IDE help but they're usually overfitted to one project style and languages. I ship quicker when I can automate the whole workflow to a series of actions and succinct results I can quickly review. And that means integrating a whole bunch of utilities to a common hub, which is usually a terminal multiplexer (Emacs also works fine for that).

Neither, I almost entirely work in a CLI. And yes it's massively more efficient, I get daily reminders as I try to coach jr engineers who stubbornly refuse to leave the comfort of their GUIs throw away hundreds of hours of productivity for fear of being slightly uncomfortable.
